title: Typography
summary: **CSS typography** is the set of properties that control how text looks and reads — the font, its size and weight, line spacing, letter spacing, alignment, and decoration. Good typography is the single biggest lever on readability and the polish of a page.

subtopics.title: font-family and font stacks
subtopics.explanation: font-family lists fonts in priority order; the browser uses the first one available and falls back to the next, ending in a generic family (serif, sans-serif, monospace). Quote multi-word names. Always provide a fallback so text still renders sensibly if your preferred font fails to load.

subtopics.title: Web fonts: @font-face and Google Fonts
subtopics.explanation: Web fonts let you ship custom typefaces. @font-face declares a font file (woff2 is the modern format) and names it for use in font-family. Google Fonts is a hosted shortcut: you add a <link> in HTML (or @import in CSS) and then reference the family. Self-hosting woff2 with font-display: swap is faster and more private.

subtopics.title: font-size
subtopics.explanation: font-size sets text size. px is fixed; rem scales with the root font-size and is preferred for accessibility because it respects the user's browser settings. em is relative to the parent's font-size and compounds when nested. A common base is 16px (1rem).

subtopics.title: font-weight and font-style
subtopics.explanation: font-weight controls thickness: keywords normal (400) and bold (700), or numeric 100-900. font-style is mostly normal vs italic. The weight you can actually render depends on which weights of the font you loaded — asking for 600 with only 400/700 loaded gives a faux bold.

subtopics.title: line-height
subtopics.explanation: line-height sets the vertical space each line occupies, driving readability. A unitless value (e.g. 1.5) is best practice because it scales with the element's font-size and inherits cleanly. Body text usually wants 1.4-1.7; tight headings can go lower.

subtopics.title: letter-spacing and word-spacing
subtopics.explanation: letter-spacing adjusts the gap between characters (tracking) and word-spacing the gap between words. Slight positive tracking can help uppercase headings; negative tracking can tighten large display text. Use sparingly on body copy — too much hurts readability.

subtopics.title: text-align, text-decoration, text-transform
subtopics.explanation: text-align positions inline text (left, right, center, justify). text-decoration adds/removes underline, overline, line-through — commonly used to control link underlines. text-transform changes case visually (uppercase, lowercase, capitalize) without altering the underlying text.

subtopics.title: System font stack and readability
subtopics.explanation: The system font stack uses the OS's native UI font, so text loads instantly with zero download and looks at home on each platform. Combined with comfortable line-height, sensible measure (line length ~45-75 characters), and adequate contrast, it produces fast, highly readable text.
subtopics.example: font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;

foundations.overview: Typography in CSS is how you turn raw text into something legible and on-brand. A handful of properties — font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, letter-spacing, and the text-* properties — cover the vast majority of real work. Because text is the bulk of most pages, small typographic choices have an outsized effect on how professional and readable a site feels.
foundations.formalDefinition: CSS typography is the collection of font and text properties that determine the typeface, size, weight, style, spacing, alignment, decoration, and casing of rendered text, plus the mechanisms (font stacks, @font-face, font-display) for loading and falling back between fonts.
foundations.whyItMatters: Readable, consistent text is the foundation of usable UI. Poor typography (cramped line-height, low contrast, the wrong fallback font) makes content hard to read and a product feel unpolished, while good typography improves comprehension and trust.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of font-family as a fallback chain the browser walks until it finds a font it has, and the other properties as knobs on that text: size, thickness, vertical rhythm (line-height), horizontal spacing (letter/word-spacing), and presentation (align/decoration/transform).
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser matches font-family against installed and loaded fonts, downloads web fonts, then shapes and lays out glyphs during layout. font-display decides what shows while a web font loads (e.g. swap shows fallback text immediately, avoiding invisible text).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Setting a base font and line-height on body, scaling headings with rem, loading a brand font via woff2, styling links by toggling text-decoration, and uppercasing eyebrow labels with text-transform are everyday tasks.
foundations.businessImpact: Typography is brand: consistent type builds recognition and trust, and faster-loading fonts (woff2, font-display: swap, system stacks) reduce bounce by avoiding blank or flashing text.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Centralizing type choices in variables/tokens (sizes, weights, line-heights) keeps a codebase consistent and easy to restyle, and unitless line-height plus rem sizing avoid a class of nesting and accessibility bugs.
foundations.performanceImpact: Web fonts add network weight; using woff2, subsetting characters, preloading the critical font, and font-display: swap minimize layout shift and blocked rendering. The system font stack costs nothing to download.
commonUseCases: Setting a readable base: font-family, font-size, and line-height on body
Scaling a heading hierarchy with rem-based font-size and font-weight
Loading a brand font with @font-face (woff2) or Google Fonts
Controlling link underlines via text-decoration and styling eyebrow labels with text-transform

commonMisconceptions.myth: px is fine for font-size everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.reality: rem respects the user's browser font-size setting, so it's more accessible; px ignores it. Prefer rem for type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: line-height should always have a unit like 24px.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A unitless line-height (e.g. 1.5) scales with font-size and inherits cleanly; fixed units can break when font-size changes.

steps.title: Pick the first available
steps.description: It uses the first font that's installed or loaded; if Inter is missing it tries Helvetica Neue, then Arial.

steps.title: Fall back to the generic family
steps.description: If none match, it uses the generic keyword (sans-serif) so text still renders sensibly.

steps.description: line-height sets vertical rhythm; letter-spacing and word-spacing tune horizontal gaps.

steps.title: Apply presentation
steps.description: text-align, text-decoration, and text-transform finalize alignment, underlines, and casing.

debuggingLab.title: The custom font isn't applying
debuggingLab.symptom: The page still shows the default font even though Inter is loaded with @font-face.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: font-family is a comma-separated list. "Inter sans-serif" with no comma is parsed as a single (invalid) font name, so the declaration is ignored and the browser falls back to its default. It must be: font-family: "Inter", sans-serif;
commonMistakes: Omitting the comma between font names in font-family.
Forgetting a generic fallback (sans-serif) at the end of the stack.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Fix the font-family declaration so Inter is used with a proper fallback.

theory.question: What is a font stack and why do you always include a fallback?
theory.directAnswer: A font stack is the prioritized list in font-family. The browser uses the first font it has available and falls through to the next, ending in a generic family. You always include fallbacks so text still renders in a sensible font if your preferred or web font fails to load.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An ordered list of typefaces ending in a generic keyword like serif, sans-serif, or monospace.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Not every device has every font, and web fonts can fail or be slow, so a fallback chain guarantees readable text.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser checks each name left to right against installed/loaded fonts and uses the first match; the generic keyword is the guaranteed final fallback.

theory.whyImportant: Missing fallbacks lead to broken-looking or invisible text, especially on slow connections — a common, avoidable bug.
theory.realWorldExample: font-family: "Inter", "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif tries Inter first and degrades gracefully to a system sans-serif.

nestedTopics.title: Generic families
nestedTopics.explanation: serif, sans-serif, monospace, cursive, system-ui are guaranteed keywords.

nestedTopics.title: Quoting names
nestedTopics.explanation: Multi-word font names must be quoted, e.g. "Helvetica Neue".

nestedTopics.title: System font stack
nestedTopics.explanation: Uses the OS UI font for instant, native-looking text.

followUps.question: What does the generic keyword at the end do?
followUps.answer: It's the guaranteed fallback the browser maps to one of its built-in fonts if nothing else matched.

followUps.question: Why quote multi-word font names?
followUps.answer: To parse them as one font name rather than separate tokens, e.g. "Segoe UI".

theory.question: Why prefer a unitless line-height and rem for font-size?
theory.directAnswer: A unitless line-height (e.g. 1.5) is a multiplier of the element's own font-size, so it scales correctly and inherits cleanly into nested elements. rem font-sizes are relative to the root, respecting the user's browser font-size setting, which makes type accessible and consistent.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: line-height as a number (multiplier) and font-size in rem (root-relative units).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To keep vertical rhythm and sizing proportional and user-respecting instead of brittle and fixed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Unitless line-height multiplies the current font-size at each element; rem multiplies the root font-size, which the user can change.

theory.whyImportant: These choices prevent accessibility and inheritance bugs that fixed px values cause.
theory.realWorldExample: Body line-height: 1.6 with h1 font-size: 2rem keeps spacing proportional even when the heading is larger.

nestedTopics.title: em vs rem
nestedTopics.explanation: em is relative to the parent and compounds when nested; rem is relative to the root.

nestedTopics.title: Fixed line-height pitfalls
nestedTopics.explanation: A px line-height doesn't scale if font-size changes, cramping text.

nestedTopics.title: User settings
nestedTopics.explanation: rem honors the browser's default font-size for accessibility.

followUps.question: What's the difference between em and rem?
followUps.answer: em is relative to the parent element's font-size and compounds; rem is always relative to the root font-size.

scenario.question: Users see blank text for a second before your custom font appears, causing layout shift. How do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: That's the flash of invisible text (FOIT). Set font-display: swap (or optional) in @font-face so the browser shows the fallback immediately and swaps in the web font when ready, and preload the critical font. Using woff2 and subsetting reduces the wait.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A font-loading behavior where text is hidden until the web font downloads.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The default block period hides text to avoid a visible swap, but that means blank text on slow networks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: font-display: swap renders fallback text first, then swaps; <link rel="preload"> fetches the font earlier.

scenario.whyImportant: Invisible text and layout shift hurt perceived performance and Core Web Vitals.

nestedTopics.title: font-display values
nestedTopics.explanation: auto, block, swap, fallback, optional trade off blank time vs swap.

nestedTopics.title: Preloading
nestedTopics.explanation: Preload the woff2 to start the download sooner.

followUps.question: How do you reduce layout shift from the font swap?
followUps.answer: Pick a fallback with similar metrics (or use size-adjust / ascent-override) so the fallback and web font occupy similar space.

coding.question: Write CSS that loads a custom font with @font-face and applies a readable body type scale.
coding.thoughtProcess: Declare the font with @font-face using woff2 and font-display: swap so text isn't invisible while loading. Then set a system-ish stack starting with the custom font, a base rem size, and a unitless line-height for readability.
coding.lineByLine: @font-face names the Inter font and points to a woff2 file; font-display: swap shows fallback text immediately. body uses Inter first with system-ui/sans-serif fallbacks, a 1rem base, and unitless 1.6 line-height. h1 scales up to 2rem with a tighter heading line-height.

alternativeApproaches.title: Google Fonts link
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Skip @font-face and add a <link> to Google Fonts, then reference the family.
alternativeApproaches.code:
/* in HTML head */ /* <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter&display=swap" rel="stylesheet"> */
body { font-family: "Inter", sans-serif; }

followUps.question: How do you make this faster?
followUps.answer: Self-host woff2, subset to the characters you use, and preload the critical font file.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Typography lives in a small set of tokens — font families, a modular size scale, weights, and line-heights — usually as CSS custom properties applied at :root and referenced everywhere. Components consume tokens rather than hardcoding values, so the whole site can be restyled centrally.
productionDeepDive.performance: Web fonts are a top performance cost. Use woff2, subset glyphs, limit weights, preload the critical font, and set font-display: swap to avoid invisible text. The system font stack is the zero-cost baseline when brand isn't critical.
productionDeepDive.security: Fonts loaded from third parties (e.g. Google Fonts) add a request to an external origin with privacy implications; self-hosting avoids leaking user data and removes a third-party dependency. Use Subresource Integrity / CSP where appropriate.
productionDeepDive.scaling: A documented type scale and named text styles (display, heading, body, caption) keep typography consistent across teams and products and make redesigns a token change rather than a sweep.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Centralize sizes, weights, and line-heights as variables; prefer rem and unitless line-height so changes propagate predictably and respect user settings.
productionDeepDive.observability: Lighthouse and Web Vitals flag font-related issues like layout shift (CLS) and blocked rendering; DevTools shows which fonts loaded and which fell back.

caseStudies.problem: Brand web fonts caused invisible text and layout shift on slow networks.
caseStudies.solution: Self-hosted subsetted woff2 with font-display: swap and a preload of the primary font.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A brief flash of fallback text in exchange for always-visible content.
caseStudies.lessons: Visible fallback text beats blank text; metric-matched fallbacks minimize the swap shift.

keyTakeaways: font-family is a fallback chain: list preferred fonts first and always end in a generic family.
Prefer rem for font-size (respects user settings) and a unitless line-height (scales and inherits cleanly).
Load web fonts with woff2 and font-display: swap to avoid invisible text and reduce layout shift.
Use text-align, text-decoration, and text-transform for alignment, underlines, and casing; tune letter/word-spacing sparingly.
The system font stack gives fast, native, zero-download text — a great default when brand fonts aren't essential.
